title: Local Gaussian bounds on the non-destructive discrimination of two-mode squeezed states
authors: Mi-Jung So, James Moran, Youngrong Lim, Mahn-Soo Choi, Hyukjoon Kwon
abstract: Typical measurement setups in quantum systems are destructive, meaning that states are irretrievably altered after measurement. In this work, we analyse non-destructive discrimination of two two-mode squeezed vacuum states using local Gaussian measurements. We investigate a tradeoff relation between the success probability of discrimination and the fidelity of the resulting state with the initial state, and construct a protocol given by local Gaussian measurements, which is optimal within our numerically explored class. We also extend to the case where we allow for additional pre-shared entanglement, and show that this regime allows us to exceed the standard local Gaussian bound for the fidelity-success probability tradeoff. Our work provides a natural extension of the tradeoff between information gain and disturbance in entangled-state discrimination, previously established for finite-dimensional quantum systems, to infinite-dimensional continuous-variable systems.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to quantify the trade-off between successfully identifying a quantum state and disturbing it during the measurement process. It focuses on two-mode squeezed vacuum states using local Gaussian measurements. The key finding is that incorporating pre-shared entanglement can enhance discrimination beyond the standard theoretical limits.
main_problem: The work analyzes the non-destructive discrimination of two-mode squeezed vacuum (TMSV) states using local Gaussian measurements.
main_result: The authors establish an explicit tradeoff relation between success probability and measurement-induced disturbance, and show that pre-shared entanglement allows exceeding the standard local Gaussian bound.
method: The analysis involves deriving the success probability and fidelity using Gaussian state theory, optimizing a score function ($P \cdot F$), and comparing different measurement protocols.
model_or_system: The system involves two-mode squeezed vacuum states, which are continuous-variable (CV) Gaussian states. The process is modeled using local Gaussian measurements and potentially pre-shared entanglement.
key_observables: Success Probability ($P$), Fidelity ($F$), and the combined score function ($P \cdot F$).
important_parameters: Squeezing Parameter ($\lambda$), beamsplitter angle ($	heta$), and the strength of pre-shared entanglement.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the GLOCC1 class (at most one adaptive stage) for the primary bound derivation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the general local Gaussian circuit for discrimination, comparing performance across different measurement schemes (simplest vs. displacement vs. squeezing) as a function of the beam splitter angle $	heta$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework for local Gaussian discrimination, then optimizing the score function $P \cdot F$ for various measurement strategies, and finally deriving the optimal trade-off relation.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial infinite-dimensional generalization of the information-disturbance tradeoff, extending established concepts from finite-dimensional quantum systems to continuous-variable quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. General local Gaussian circuit with one adap- tive stage for the non-destructive discrimination of two-mode squeezed vacua. Each party mixes the received signal mode (1 or 2) with an ancillary mode (3 or 4) on a local beamsplitter of angle θ, performs homodyne detection on the ancillary output to obtain M = {x3, x4}, and—conditioned on the classically communicated outcomes—applies a single-mode Gaussian op- eration ˆUGi(M) to the surviving signal mode.

FIG. 2. Simplest scheme with an initial TMSV state | ± λ⟩ prepared by Charlie and distributed to Alice (left) and Bob (right). Each party mixes the received mode with an auxiliary vacuum mode |0⟩using a local beamsplitter with parameter θ. Both parties then perform homodyne detection on one of the output modes, producing outcomes x3 and x4, while the remaining mode forms the post-measurement state used for the fidelity readout. We collect these outcomes into the classical set M = {x3, x4}. This corresponds to choosing l = 0 and ˆUGi(M) = I, the identity operator, in the general circuit.

FIG. 3. Success probabilities of the simplest scheme (Fig. 2) and the measurement-based displacement circuit (Fig. 4), as functions of θ for several values of λ, which coincide for the same setting with initial state (|λ⟩) and two vacuum nodes.

FIG. 4. Measurement-based displacement scheme. Con- ditioned on the set of measurement outcomes M = {x3, x4} obtained on modes 3 and 4, the displacement gates ˆD (αi(M)) (i = 1, 2) shift the post-measurement state to the phase-space origin, rendering the output fidelity indepen- dent of M and optimal. This corresponds to choosing l = 0 and ˆUGi(M) = ˆD(αi(M)) in the general circuit.

FIG. 5. Fidelity as a function of θ for the simplest scheme (Fig. 2) and the measurement-based displacement circuit (Fig. 4), shown for several values of λ. Each value of λ is repre- sented by a distinct color, with the dashed and solid curves of the same color corresponding to the simplest scheme and the measurement-based displacement circuit, respectively. The latter consistently achieves higher fidelity, demonstrating the advantage of this approach.
